reference.source: Greenspan, Orthopedic Imaging: A Practical Approach
clinicalPearls: One of the most common incidental bone lesions of childhood and adolescence, typically found in the metaphysis of long bones about the knee (distal femur, proximal and distal tibia).

The small purely cortical form is termed a fibrous cortical defect, whereas the larger lesion extending into the medullary cavity is called a non-ossifying fibroma; they represent a spectrum of the same process.
Radiographs show an eccentric, cortically based, well-defined lucent lesion with a thin sclerotic scalloped or grape-cluster margin and its long axis parallel to the shaft.
It is a classic do-not-touch or leave-me-alone lesion; imaging is diagnostic and biopsy of a typical lesion is unnecessary.
Most lesions regress spontaneously and ossify from the diaphyseal side with skeletal maturation, becoming uncommon after early adulthood.
Large lesions occupying more than roughly half the transverse diameter of the bone carry a risk of pathological fracture and may warrant curettage and grafting.
Multiple non-ossifying fibromas with extraskeletal features (cafe-au-lait macules, learning difficulty, hypogonadism, ocular and cardiovascular anomalies) constitute Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome.
An association with neurofibromatosis type 1 should be considered when lesions are multiple.
reference.pathophysiology: Non-ossifying fibroma is a benign, developmental, non-neoplastic fibrous lesion rather than a true tumour, believed to arise near the physis and to migrate away from the growth plate into the metaphysis and diaphysis as the bone lengthens. Histologically it consists of a cellular proliferation of bland spindle-shaped fibroblasts arranged in a storiform (whorled) pattern, admixed with lipid-laden foam cells, scattered multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells and haemosiderin deposition, accounting for the alternative name fibroxanthoma. The lesion is self-limiting and resolves through progressive ossification and remodelling, so that most examples heal spontaneously by the end of the second decade.
additionalDifferentials: Giant cell tumour (in the skeletally mature)
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs, which are usually diagnostic on their own
MRI reserved for atypical appearances or diagnostic uncertainty
CT to assess cortical thinning and fracture risk in large lesions
Clinical assessment for cafe-au-lait macules and other features of neurofibromatosis type 1 or Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome
Interval follow-up radiographs to confirm expected regression and ossification
Biopsy only in genuinely atypical lesions, since it is not required for classic ones
redFlags: Pain in the absence of a pathological fracture
Rapid or unexpected enlargement of the lesion
Cortical breach or an associated soft-tissue mass
Size approaching the threshold for pathological fracture in a weight-bearing bone
Atypical location such as the axial skeleton or a flat bone
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, with spontaneous resolution the rule and a very low recurrence rate after curettage of large or fractured lesions. Malignant potential is essentially absent.
pitfalls: Performing an unnecessary biopsy of a radiographically classic lesion
Misinterpreting a benign lesion as an aggressive or malignant tumour
Underestimating the fracture risk of a large lesion in a weight-bearing bone
Overlooking a syndromic association when lesions are multiple
references: Greenspan, Orthopedic Imaging: A Practical Approach
WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone (current edition)
Resnick, Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Manage the typical asymptomatic lesion conservatively, as this is a classic leave-alone lesion requiring no intervention
Avoid biopsy of radiologically classic lesions, since plain radiographs alone are diagnostic
Confirm the expected spontaneous regression and ossification with interval follow-up radiographs through skeletal maturation
Assess large lesions occupying much of the transverse bone width with CT for cortical thinning and pathological fracture risk
Offer curettage and bone grafting, with internal fixation, for large lesions at fracture risk or after a pathological fracture
Advise activity modification or protected weight-bearing where a substantial lesion threatens fracture
Evaluate for café-au-lait macules and features of neurofibromatosis type 1 or Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome when lesions are multiple
